finding.claim: The unauthenticated POST /hooks/test handler passes a user-supplied callback URL straight to axios.post. The server will POST to any host, scheme, or port the caller chooses. That includes internal services and cloud metadata such as 169.254.169.254. Axios follows redirects by default, and the response status is returned to the caller, so the caller can probe internal hosts. The router is named `pub`; the file does not show how it is mounted, so I did not confirm that no authentication is applied upstream.
finding.source: req.body.callback (JSON or form body of POST /hooks/test)

trace.note: pub.post('/hooks/test') handler registered on the public router with no auth middleware; requireAdmin is applied only to the admin router
req.body.callback goes unmodified into axios.post as the URL
The upstream status code is returned in the JSON response, which gives the attacker an oracle for open and closed internal ports

finding.guards_checked: No scheme, host or IP allowlist or blocklist. No DNS resolution check. No redirect restriction (axios maxRedirects defaults to 5). No authentication on the pub router within this file. The only guard in the file is requireAdmin, and it applies to the admin router only.

verdict.reason: routes.js:19-21 registers pub.post('/hooks/test') with no auth middleware (requireAdmin at routes.js:12 applies only to the admin router), and routes.js:20 passes req.body.callback unvalidated to axios.post, with the status returned at routes.js:21; the only other file is absent, so upstream mounting auth can't be ruled out, but nothing in the code available restricts it.

finding.claim: The admin-only GET /diagnostics/fetch endpoint fetches an arbitrary URL taken from the query string with axios.get. There is no destination validation, so an admin, or anyone who hijacks an admin session through CSRF or XSS, can reach internal services and cloud metadata. Impact is lower than ssrf-1 because it requires the admin role. It is still a full-read-style SSRF primitive, since axios follows redirects and the status is returned.

trace.note: admin.use(requireAdmin) gates the router on session.role === 'admin'
The response status is returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: requireAdmin (routes.js:7-10) restricts access to session.role === 'admin'. This is an authorization check only and does not constrain the destination. No scheme, host or IP allowlist. No DNS pinning. Redirects are followed. The session and role are not set in this file, so I could not check whether they are trustworthy.

verdict.guard_found: requireAdmin (routes.js:7-10, applied at :12) only checks session.role === 'admin'; no destination validation (scheme/host/IP allowlist) before axios.get at :15
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate, but the req.query.url that reaches axios.get at routes.js:15 can only be supplied by an authenticated admin because requireAdmin at routes.js:7-12 returns 403 to everyone else, so it is not controllable by an unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker (the CSRF/XSS route is speculative, with nothing in this file showing it, and the response only exposes status at :16).
